The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

The US knew there was a threat to RAF Fairford - that's not in dispute here. The FPCON changes, armed patrol vehicles inside the base and concrete barricades all show that.

It seems possible to me that perhaps these 5 lads (or 8-10 if the eyewitness farmer is correct) were not actually there to attack the base - perhaps (given the fake fuel vans) they were actually in the area trying to steal fuel from local vehicles.

The farmer sees it, calls police. Police (who likely were aware of the USAF concerns) swarm into the area having perhaps not expected the "attackers" so soon. They manage to arrest 5 suspects and treat the 3 vans with every necessary precaution (as they should) - evacuating the neighbourhood, bringing Army EOD in, etc.

The males are initially arrested for Explosives Act offences (pending a safe way to check inside the vans) & go to custody. In the circumstances, further arrested for the Terrorism Act offence. However, after seizing whatever evidence they could (and examining the vans), it looks like police may have determined these aren't the attackers - as I say, potentially fuel thieves in the wrong place at the wrong time?

It's worth noting that if the terrorism act offences were looking likely, police could keep them detained for 48hrs initially before requiring a court to approve a longer period of time. Alternatively under normal arrest powers contained within the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, they can be held for 24hrs initially (extended to 36hrs under authority of a Police Superintendent if specific requirements are met), and up to 72hrs if a further extension is authorised by a court. Now clearly if they were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning and conveyed either to a local custody, or a dedicated counter-terrorism custody (likely closest in London), the fact they've been bailed today suggests they've spent at most 24-30hrs in custody before evidential review officers and the Crown Prosecution Service have determined there is insufficient evidence to charge them with an offence right now.

So they bail them with conditions not to contact each other as is normal procedure for vehicle interference/theft offences like that. But police need to download and analyse phones, and anything potentially seized from home addresses in order to ensure no link to the Iranian government or IRGC.

Meanwhile, did the actual planned attack get foiled inadvertently? Perhaps? Trump told the world that the US had been monitoring the "attackers" for some time - I'd suggest that if these lads genuinely were just in the wrong place at the wrong time, the actual suspects are now staying hidden until this all blows over a bit.

Either way, we don't have all the facts and that's part of any criminal or CT investigation - so yes, it sounds bad and arguably CTP could have done a better job of explaining it to the public, but they have to play their cards close to their chest right now in case my guesswork here is right and the suspects are still out there somewhere.

ECI’S NEW SIR ORDERS: A COURSE CORRECTION — OR A RESPONSE TO THE QUESTIONS?

The Election Commission’s latest press note introduces several important changes to the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process.

Most significantly, voters who receive notices for being “unmapped” or having “logical discrepancies” will no longer ordinarily be required to appear personally before the ERO. Booth Level Officers (BLOs) will visit their homes, collect documents and upload them on ECINet. Hearings will be held only in exceptional circumstances, preferably online. 

The Commission has also directed District Election Officers to establish help desks and special camps for night-shelter residents, labourers, poor and homeless citizens—groups for whom documentation and physical appearances can create particular difficulties.

Another significant decision is the extension of the claims-and-objections period in Delhi up to 30 October 2026, with disposal extended to 30 November. Maharashtra has also received an extension, with claims and objections permitted until 12 October and disposal until 10 November, according to the Commission’s press note.

The ECI has further announced an independent expert review of ECINet, involving an expert from IIT/IIM, to examine whether the system complies with the relevant Acts and Rules.

But the timing is important.

Just days earlier, The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections on at least 14 occasions concerning aspects of the SIR process, including voter additions/deletions and access to electoral data. 

The Election Commission has rejected the characterization of these differences as institutional dissent, maintaining that final decisions—including SIR—were taken unanimously by the full Commission. The 26 September press note reiterates that position. 

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court, during proceedings on Delhi SIR on 22 September, questioned the process by which “logical discrepancy” notices were being generated and asked the ECI to consider additional safeguards and clearer guidance for affected voters. 

So the real issue is not simply whether the ECI has changed its procedure.

It is whether these changes will make the process more transparent, accessible and demonstrably protective of every eligible voter’s right to remain on the electoral roll.

A notice should not become a barrier to voting.
A software-generated discrepancy should not become a substitute for human verification.
And every eligible citizen must have a meaningful opportunity to establish their right to vote.

The credibility of SIR will ultimately depend not merely on the number of names added or removed, but on whether every eligible voter can understand, challenge and correct the process affecting their franchise.

Source: Election Commission of India Press Note No. ECI/PN/120/2026, dated 26 September 2026.

text:
grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

In Portland, Oregon, there’s a small coffee shop called Cozy Bean.

During the day, it’s what you’d expect—people stopping in for a hot drink, soft background music, the usual warmth of a neighborhood café.

But something unexpected happens after closing time.

Once the customers leave and the lights are turned off, the owner turns them back on—but not for more business. He opens the doors again, this time for a different kind of guest: street dogs.

Since 2018, Cozy Bean has quietly offered shelter to stray dogs in the area. There's no advertising, no big signs, no posts asking for attention. It’s just something the owner does—every single night.

Inside, he sets out old blankets, cushions, and bowls of clean water. The dogs come in from the cold, some limping, some soaked from the rain, and they find a place to rest. They aren’t locked in or forced to stay. They just know they’re welcome—and they settle in like they belong there.

Some of the dogs are regulars. Others come and go. But every night, they have somewhere safe to sleep. A break from the noise and danger of the street.
The owner doesn’t do interviews. He doesn’t expect anything in return. He just makes space for those that have none.

It’s a simple act—opening a door, turning on a light, offering a little comfort. But it shows a level of compassion that’s hard to find in today’s world.

This isn’t about saving the world. It’s about doing what you can, right where you are. And that, in its quiet way, is something extraordinary.

text:
**Illegal Monday** 
The type of white paper that launched the account. Long post. Citations at end.

Why Tech Workers Fighting Visas Cannot Afford to Dismiss Illegal Immigration

Six arguments, one labor market, and the illegal labor that does not file an LCA

Chief Engineer | September 2026 | Evidence brief for intelligent followers. tl;dr can move along. Not a press release.

Abstract:
Tech workers have a clean target in the H-1B system because the government publishes the filings. That visibility is useful and incomplete. Unauthorized labor is larger, harder to count, and already inside industries that look corporate on a W-2. This brief lays out six reasons visa-focused workers should treat illegal immigration as a first-order problem: one labor market, housing and schools, shared document fraud, political headcount, the collapse of high-trust work, and a hidden office pipeline that never appears in lottery data. The strongest claim is the last one. Visas have a database. Illegal office labor has a stolen Social Security number and an I-9 a manager certified as genuine.

Introduction
H-1B is measurable. In fiscal year 2024, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services approved 399,395 H-1B petitions. Seventy-one percent of those beneficiaries were born in India (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, 2025). Engineers can name the vendors, pull Labor Condition Applications, and argue about wages. Unauthorized presence does not come with that dashboard.

Pew Research Center estimated 14 million unauthorized immigrants in the United States in 2023, with 9.7 million in the workforce, 5.6 percent of all U.S. workers (Passel and Krogstad, 2025). Professional and business services, the industry bucket that includes staffing, contractors, and back-office work next to engineers, ran about 7 percent unauthorized in 2023 (Passel and Krogstad, 2025).
Treat that 14 million figure as real. At that scale the implication for American tech labor is horrific. No exaggeration.

Set aside agriculture and construction for a moment. Those still hurt tech workers. That is another post.
The six arguments below are not separate crusades. They are one system viewed from the desk of a worker who already knows the visa fight and has been told the other fight is someone else's problem.

Too many comments read: I don't care about illegals. That is ignorance on display.

Here is why.

The Six Arguments
The labor pool is one market

Visa fights decide who sits in the cube. Illegal hiring decides what the floor under that cube costs. Unauthorized workers were 15 percent of construction and 14 percent of agriculture in 2023, and 8 percent of leisure and hospitality (Passel and Krogstad, 2025). Those trades set local wages, housing starts, food prices, and logistics costs in the same metros that absorbed H-1B growth. Employers who can tap an unauthorized pool do not compete as hard for legal labor anywhere on the wage ladder. Calling the result a labor shortage is a slogan. It is a suppressed reservation wage. A tech worker who only audits the lottery is measuring the labeled pipe and ignoring the unlabeled one that still moves the cost of living.

Housing and schools are not a side issue

Nominal tech pay looks high until rent, property tax, classroom size, and emergency-room wait times eat it. Unauthorized households concentrate in the same states that already run large Indian and other visa populations: California, Texas, New Jersey, and similar hubs (Passel and Krogstad, 2025; Ward and Batalova, 2026). School districts enroll first and match immigration files later, if they match them at all. A B-2 visitor is not authorized to use public K-12 as a regular student under federal rules, yet local practice often treats presence as residency (Immigration and Nationality Act section 214(m)). Visa reform that leaves interior status unenforced does not save the school or the starter home. This rearranges who gets the scarce seat.

Status fraud is the same picture

Overstaying a tourist visa, working after a petition dies, using a stolen Social Security number, and sitting on a B-2 while relatives work are not a different moral category from H-1B abuse. They are the same failure: nobody matches the body to the file. Form I-9 requires the employer to examine documents and certify, under penalty of law, that they appear genuine and relate to the person (8 U.S.C. section 1324a). Repeated I-9 failure, identity theft on a payroll, and vendor layers that hide the worker are how both the staffing firm and the cash crew stay in business.

ICE worksite cases keep finding stolen numbers used for wages and benefits (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 2025; U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 2026). If the shop is never reported, neither lane to these jobs gets cut.

Politics follows headcount, not job titles

Sanctuary rules, benefit access, driver's licenses, and census apportionment are driven by the large unauthorized population, not by the annual H-1B cap. Pew's 14 million figure for 2023, with about 6 million holding some temporary protection and about 8 million holding none, is a political mass (Passel and Krogstad, 2025). ICE manpower is finite. A force on the order of 22,000 agents cannot do worksite, street, and jail detainers at once. The cheap-labor lobby uses both the visa statute and the unenforced interior to exploit the resource for profit. Split the issue into "skilled good, illegal other" and the same donors keep E-Verify voluntary and interior enforcement thin. Tech workers still pay the coalition that protects both pipelines.

High-trust work dies when the surrounding county is low-trust

Engineering assumes contracts, credentials, and a common language in the meeting. A county that will not remove a known unauthorized crime family, or a hospital that staffs people who cannot communicate a consent, is not a county that stays good at intellectual property and quality control. Multi-generational American workers, including Hispanic families with roots older than living memory, are not the problem. The problem is a system that treats status as optional and undeserved while expecting the office to remain high-trust. You cannot run a specialty-occupation economy on I-9 theater and hope the schools, jails, and clinics stay someone else's responsibility.

The hidden corporate path for illegal employees is larger in uncertainty than the lottery

H-1B is apparent to us because Labor Condition Applications and petition counts are public. Unauthorized corporate labor does not file an LCA. It files an I-9 with a stolen number that belongs to a citizen, a child, or a dead account, or it keeps a badge after OPT or H-1B status expires. The Social Security Administration has long documented name-number mismatches and SSN misuse by noncitizens not authorized to work (Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General, 2004). Later estimates put millions of unauthorized workers on valid or borrowed numbers in some years, with the Earnings Suspense File holding unmatched wages at enormous scale.

ICE's Glenn Valley Foods operation found about 70 illegal aliens using stolen identities and more than 100 citizen victims whose prescriptions, disability checks, taxes, and licenses were wrecked (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 2025). A Kentucky window plant produced indictments for stolen numbers on I-9s (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 2026). From the next desk that person looks like a coworker. From USCIS they are out of status. There is no public headcount of unauthorized workers in software, help desk, or vendor IT. That gap is the point. Absence of a lottery table is not absence of bodies.

The Strongest Argument**

The strongest argument is not that every engineer should stop caring about H-1B. The strongest argument is that H-1B is just one labeled slice of a substitution system made up of many others, and the unlabeled slice sits in the same buildings.

A lottery you can screenshot will always attract more heat than a stolen SSN on a W-2. That is a measurement error, not a conclusion about harm.

Most do not realize it, but these illegal aliens are in tech and management jobs. By the numbers which are certainly understated... millions of them- they just aren't filing their job or foreign college on a register that we can see but they are web developers, programmers, MBA, and scientists all the same. There is almost no occupation untaught in a foreign country that hasn't been found to be employed in the USA illegally. 

Professional and business services already carried a 7 percent unauthorized share in 2023 (Passel and Krogstad, 2025). Identity-theft worksite cases prove the method for getting onto formal payroll. Status rot (overstay, lapsed petition, B-2 plus remote work) proves the method for staying off the H-1B list while keeping the badge. Employers certify documents. Vendors hide the headcount. Citizens absorb the tax and credit damage when the number was stolen, with no voice to make it public. Tech workers who treat illegal presence as a blue-collar story are volunteering to miss the massive number of jobs that are theirs.

If the standard is "show me the LCA," the unauthorized office worker will always win the argument by disappearing. The correct standard is whether the person is authorized to work. That question belongs to ICE, USCIS, and the Department of Labor, and it only gets asked when someone reports what they saw.

Summation
What this brief established is simple. Visa abuse is real, documented, and concentrated. The visa system itself is abusive to our unemployed degreed labor. It attracts the majority of attention.

This is hard to accept but has to be understood.

Unauthorized presence is larger, less visible, and already inside industries that are not farms. One labor market means construction and hospitality wages still move the cost of living for engineers. Imagine if competition for employees pushed wages to 30 dollars per hour to match inflation. Where would an engineering salary lie? Document fraud and weak I-9s are all in the same bucket. 

Political power tracks bodies, not job codes, and they profit off the capital with Chamber of Commerce money greasing the cheap-labor transactions that sell out our prosperity.

High-trust work cannot be isolated from the country that refuses to enforce status. The hidden corporate pipeline is the piece visa activists are most likely to miss.

The practical implication is not to abandon H-1B reform. It is to stop treating interior enforcement as a lower-class errand. Report unauthorized hiring. Demand E-Verify with teeth. Treat overstay and stolen-identity payroll as illegal employment, because that is what the statute already says. The laws are there and we should push for enforcement of every single statute. The harm is generational and lowers the potential of our society through a cash-out dilution. A specialty-occupation workforce that only polices the lottery will keep losing to the underground illegal system that never files one.

References
8 U.S.C. section 1324a. Unlawful employment of aliens.
Immigration and Nationality Act section 214(m), 8 U.S.C. section 1184(m). Limitation on public school attendance for certain nonimmigrants.
Passel, J. S., and Krogstad, J. M. (2025, August 21). U.S. unauthorized immigrant population reached a record 14 million in 2023. Pew Research Center.
Social Security Administration, Office of the Inspector General. (2004). Social Security numbers: Noncitizens with earnings and unauthorized work (A-03-04-14037).
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. (2025). Characteristics of H-1B specialty occupation workers: Fiscal year 2024 annual report to Congress.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. (2025, June 18). ICE worksite enforcement operation uncovers widespread identity theft affecting more than 100 victims across the nation.
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. (2026, June 17). Fraud crackdown: 13 illegal aliens arrested, 8 indicted for using stolen Social Security numbers to work in Kentucky.
Ward, N., and Batalova, J. (2026). Indian immigrants in the United States. Migration Policy Institute.
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. (2026). Advisory on financial activity associated with non-work-authorized populations.

This brief is for public discussion on Illegal Monday. It is not legal advice. Report suspected unauthorized employment to ICE (866-347-2423 or ) and suspected visa or petition fraud to USCIS.

Bookmark this. Share or quote it. Comment if you have watched an office treat illegal presence as someone else's problem. 

Follow for more Illegal Monday.

text: Share her story. Emme’s story is powerful, and sharing it like this can save lives. In a heart-wrenching turn of events that reminds us all of the devastating consequences of impaired driving, my daughter Emme’s life was tragically cut short at just twenty-two years old. Her death was caused by a single decision made under the influence of alcohol. Today, I share her story not only as a father’s personal loss, but as a stark warning about the dangers of drinking and driving.Emme Desimoni was a proud graduate of Granite Hills High School, Class of 2019. She was the captain of the volleyball team and helped lead them to championship titles in both 2017 and 2018. She was named Libero of the Year in 2018, and her performance was so outstanding that she even made the front page of the Daily Press after beating Apple Valley High School for the first time in eleven years.Emme was a three-sport athlete — excelling in volleyball, girls’ wrestling, and track and field. She was a bright, engaged young woman who was deeply involved with her classmates, teachers, coaches, and fellow athletes — much like many of you sitting here today. Everyone thinks, “It won’t happen to me.” But it did happen to Emme.The Incident:On April 15, 2024, Emme made the fateful decision to drive after drinking alcohol. That choice ended her https://t.co/3JRPRU52HK 3:00 a.m. that morning, my wife and I received a phone call telling us our daughter had been in a terrible accident and that we needed to get to Chandler, Arizona immediately. We began a six-hour drive to the hospital. During that agonizing ride, the doctor called and asked us to pull over so he could speak with us. On the side of the I-10 freeway, he told us that Emme had been cut out of her vehicle — a process that took nearly thirty minutes with limited medical attention. He said there was nothing more they could do to save her.I will never forget the sound of my wife’s scream that morning.When we finally arrived at the hospital and walked into the ICU, the reality hit us with brutal force. My wife cried out, “No, Emme! Not my Emme!” Our beautiful daughter lay on life support. Her head had been stapled shut from the front all the way to the back. Her right eye was so swollen it bulged out of its socket. She had broken her wrist, her knee, and her C2 and C4 vertebrae. She lay there completely still, kept alive only by a ventilator.The only decision left for us was when to say https://t.co/mdEJerq57a we sat with her, telling her how much we loved her and holding her for the final hours of her life, the police arrived to update us on the investigation. Emme’s blood alcohol level was 0.16 — twice the legal limit. She had been traveling eastbound on the I-10 freeway off-ramp, ran a red light at 68 miles per hour, and slammed into the trailer of a semi-truck. She was trapped underneath it. It took emergency crews nearly thirty minutes to free her before transporting her to Chandler Trauma Center.While we were deciding when to remove life support, my wife asked for warm water and towels. In Emme’s final moments, I watched her mother gently clean our daughter’s hair with soap and water — carefully washing out pieces of glass and dried blood. It was the last thing she would ever do for her little https://t.co/Xl7Tok0Zkp I stepped out of the room, overwhelmed with grief, I saw the entire nursing staff standing there in tears, deeply moved by this tender moment between a mother and her https://t.co/5mobZTyYmV approximately 2:03 p.m., we made the heartbreaking decision to remove the ventilator. In that moment, we saw that all of Emme’s teeth had been knocked out. It took about ninety seconds for her to pass peacefully. At 2:05 p.m. on April 15, 2024, Emme Desimoni was pronounced dead.She became another statistic — one of the thousands killed every year in alcohol-related crashes. In the United States, someone dies in an alcohol-related crash every 15 minutes.

text:
Before action was taken to demolish parts of the Shahi Mosque in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, for road widening, the city’s Qazi and mosque officials reportedly asked local residents to leave the area at night by simply saying, “Go back to your homes.” However, they did not clearly inform them that parts of the mosque would be demolished in the morning.

Ujjain/Bhopal:
Tensions had been prevailing in Ujjain since Sunday night over the plan to remove a portion of the Shahi Mosque as part of an ongoing road-widening project being carried out in preparation for the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2028. Mosque committee members and religious leaders asked the people who had gathered during the night to return to their homes. However, many people alleged that they were not told that the demolition of part of the mosque would begin the following morning.
By morning, a large number of security personnel had been deployed at the site along with the administrative team and police force, and barricades were erected around the mosque. During this time, clashes between some protesters and the police were reported, including allegations of stone-pelting and the use of tear gas.
The administration says that the action to remove the portion of the mosque falling along the proposed route of the widened road is being carried out only after an order from the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The High Court had earlier dismissed two petitions, stating that the municipal corporation had followed due legal procedure.
Meanwhile, a large section of the local Muslim community said that they had merely been told to “go home” during the night, without being given details about the demolition schedule or the broader plan. As a result, many people remained near the mosque until morning, while some even spent the night inside it.

text:
IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

text:
Dear @CoinDCX Team,Ceo @smtgpt 

I am writing to raise a very serious concern regarding my recent withdrawal from CoinDCX.

=> Last month, I placed a withdrawal request (under $1000 USDT) from CoinDCX to my SBI Bank account. Despite paying all applicable taxes including 1% TDS and 28% tax (total 29%) my transaction was blocked by the bank. Later, I received both an email and a phone call instructing me to visit the bank in person. Upon visiting, I was informed that a special notice from Cyber Cell India had been issued regarding my transaction, and I was questioned about my trading history.

My questions are very clear:

1. After paying 29% tax on trading gains, why are my funds still being flagged as gambling funds or suspicious?

2. If such risks exist even after full tax compliance, should Indian users continue trusting CoinDCX, or should we simply delete the app to protect ourselves?

3. What is the meaning of a P2P exchange if, after tax deduction, withdrawals are still blocked by banks and flagged by authorities?

4. Is CoinDCX registered as a third party app with Indian banks, or why is there no direct coordination with banks to prevent such issues?

5. Why has my support ticket on this matter received no proper response so far?

—> If this problem is not addressed with a clear and transparent solution, then users will be forced to assume that CoinDCX’s P2P services are unsafe or misleading.

I request an urgent clarification from your team or leadership regarding this matter.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

is the ECI compromised?  
 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Statement on Automated Takedown of Its Instagram Posts by Meta

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restriction of its Instagram post discussing the censorship faced by digital fact-checking organisation Alt News, as well as the subsequent takedown of an Instagram Story in which https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 on 17th September 2026 had published a post highlighting the takedowns faced by Alt News in relation to its reporting on the Chauhaan film teaser. Alt News on 19th August 2026 had published a report on the content takedown they had faced, which was as follows. An Instagram post by Alt News based on the analysis of the teaser of the movie ‘Chauhaan’ was restricted by Instagram. A subsequent version was also removed, while a third version, after references to Hizbul Mujahideen militant “Burhan Wani” were removed, was allowed to remain online. Alt News also stated that search results for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram yielded no results and instead showed a message that said “these search terms may be associated with socially sensitive content”.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has been actively monitoring content takedowns through its Free Speech Tracker and had written extensively about the restrictions faced by Alt News and made a social media post discussing these particular instances to highlight the growing use of opaque content moderation systems on platforms and the chilling effect such systems can have on journalism and public-interest speech. The post specifically noted that such censorship can operate even without a formal government order, and that journalists may begin self-censoring if they believe that certain subjects, words or images could trigger restrictions.

Instagram subsequently restricted https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s posts in India. The notification stated that the content was restricted through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.” The matter became even more concerning when Scroll reported on the restrictions faced by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and Alt News in a post on Instagram. When https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter through an Instagram Story on its public handle, the Story was also taken down by Instagram through the use of automated systems.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. The lack of clarity around this notification further adds to the concern. Since the content has been taken down by automated systems it is unclear whether the restriction stems from a specific legal request or order issued to Meta, or whether Meta has restricted the content suo motu through its automated systems as part of its compliance with the due diligence requirements under the Information Technology Rules, 2021. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has not been provided with sufficient information to determine the source of the restriction, the specific legal basis for it, or the process through which the decision can be challenged.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight. This opaque suppression undermines press freedom, as well as the public’s right to reliable information, and leaves users without timely recourse to contest improper takedowns.

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the official Grievance Officer intake form for reporting does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements”. The response from the Meta AI support assistant instead asks users to physically send an email to the resident Grievance Officer, creating an entirely separate standard for reporting content takedown as opposed to other grievances. As per the Meta platforms the email available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Office report. This not only creates excessive additional friction for users, but in the case of news reporting, effectively silences journalists and curbs the spread of information for significant periods of time. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedown especially if done by automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

The Special Intensive Revision is not only about checking electoral rolls. It is also a large-scale exercise in collecting, digitising and matching personal data. When the system cannot match an elector to an old database, the burden shifts back to the individual to prove their identity, eligibility and place on the roll. (1/10)

Read more: https://t.co/2iX4uT7GnX

This creates a basic administrative question. If an elector is already on the roll, and the state’s own database or digitisation process fails to establish a match, why should the consequences of that failure fall primarily on the elector? The answer cannot simply be another form or another document. The process must account for errors in the data, the software and the administration itself. (9/10)

The SIR ultimately depends on a chain of databases, forms, photographs, mobile numbers, family linkages, legacy records and software-generated classifications. Each link can introduce an error, but the final burden is often placed on the individual whose record has been flagged. A meaningful verification process therefore requires more than notice and hearing. It requires transparency about what data is collected, how it is matched, how long it is retained, how errors are corrected and why different categories of electors appear to receive different treatment. (10/10)

text:
The software deciding who gets on India's electoral roll is a black box. ERONET was built by C-DAC, quietly handed to TCS, and the Election Commission hasn't said a word about audits, versions or updates. Even judges, ex-ministers and veterans are getting SIR notices.

We're digging in with explainers, RTIs and questions to every body involved.

The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls is being litigated as a question of the Election Commission’s powers. But behind the notices sent to millions of electors is another question that has received far less scrutiny, what software is deciding who gets flagged, on what data, and according to which rules? (1/10)
Read our full analysis: https://t.co/rvvpP20PlY

That question has now reached the Supreme Court. On 22 September, while hearing a challenge to the Delhi SIR, the Court questioned whether notices appeared to have been issued “almost mechanically” and asked the ECI to clarify the meaning of “logical discrepancy”. The Court also sought clearer guidance on what documents could resolve particular discrepancies and directed that responses should be possible through WhatsApp or email without insisting on physical appearance. (9/10)

The legal safeguards recognised by the Supreme Court require notice, an opportunity to be heard, a reasoned decision and an appeal. Those safeguards cannot operate meaningfully if the person receiving a notice does not know what rule triggered it, what data was relied upon or what evidence would address the alleged discrepancy. SIR is ultimately about electoral rights, but it is also about the software through which those rights are administered. The ECI should publish the systems, rules, audit records and operational protocols governing this process. (10/10)
